opus-5.5.text:
I think it shaped me in ways I only started to notice much later. When you start programming competitions as a kid, the first thing you learn is that a problem either has a solution or it doesn't, and the judge doesn't care how confident you feel. You submit, and you get "Accepted" or "Wrong Answer." That kind of immediate, unforgiving feedback is very humbling, and I think it trained me early on to separate what I *believe* from what I can actually *verify*.

The second thing is a habit of breaking things down. In competitions you get a problem that looks impossible at first glance, and over time you learn not to panic. You ask, what's the structure here? Is there a smaller version I can solve? Can I reduce it to something I've seen before? That way of thinking stayed with me well beyond algorithms. Even now, when I face a research question or a decision about my career, my instinct is to decompose it and look for the core constraint.

On personality, I'd say it made me fairly comfortable with being alone with a hard problem for a long time. A lot of the training is just you, a problem, and hours of being stuck. You learn to tolerate that frustration, and eventually you enjoy it a little. I think that patience is underrated.

But there were downsides too. Competitive programming rewards speed and having one correct answer, and the real world isn't like that. When I moved into research, it took me a while to adjust. In research, the hardest part is often figuring out *which question is worth asking*, not solving a well-defined one. Competitions hand you the problem; life doesn't. So I had to unlearn some of that and develop more taste and more tolerance for ambiguity.

There's also the competitive mindset itself. As a kid, you're constantly ranked, and it's easy to tie your self-worth to the scoreboard. Growing up, I had to consciously move away from that toward caring about whether the work itself is meaningful, rather than whether I beat someone.

Overall, I'm grateful for it. It gave me a strong foundation in rigorous thinking and a love of problem-solving. And honestly, many of the friends I made back then are still people I learn from today. That community may be the most lasting thing it gave me.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think the competitions shaped me more than almost anything else from that period, and not mostly in the way people assume.

The obvious part is the technical foundation. When you start doing algorithm problems at eleven or twelve, you build an intuition for complexity and structure that becomes almost physical. You look at a problem and you feel whether it's going to blow up. That's stayed with me. Even now, when I'm looking at a system or a research question, the first thing my brain does is ask what the actual bottleneck is, what grows and what doesn't.

But the deeper thing was learning to be wrong in a very precise way. In a competition, you submit, and the judge says wrong answer. It doesn't say you were close, it doesn't care that you worked hard. You just get a binary verdict. At first that's brutal for a kid. Over time it does something useful to your personality. You stop attaching your ego to whether you're right and start attaching it to how fast you can find out you're wrong. I think that's the single most valuable habit I have.

The second thing it gave me was a kind of comfort with being stuck. Most of competition time is spent staring at a problem with no idea. You learn that the feeling of having no idea isn't a signal that you should stop. It's just what the middle of thinking feels like. A lot of people never get to experience that in a safe setting, so later on when they hit a hard problem, they interpret the discomfort as "this isn't for me." I got that out of the way early.

There were costs too, I should be honest about that. Competitions reward speed and cleverness on well-defined problems, and real life mostly isn't well-defined. For a while I was too drawn to the problems that had a clean right answer and too impatient with the messy ones, the ones about people, or about what to build at all. I had to unlearn some of that. The people I most admire now are the ones who can sit with an ill-posed question for months, and that's a different muscle from the one competitions train.

And personality-wise, it made me a bit solitary early on. It's a solo sport. You sit in a room with a computer. I had to consciously learn later that the best work I've done was with other people, and that explaining something clearly is itself a form of thinking, not a tax on it.

So if I sum it up: it gave me precision, resilience, and a love of hard problems, and it gave me a few biases I've spent my adult life correcting. I'd still do it again.

astra-6.text:
I think learning to program early gave me a sense that I could figure things out for myself. You have an idea, you write something, and then the computer gives you feedback. If it doesn’t work, you have to examine your assumptions and try again. That habit—breaking a problem into smaller pieces and testing your understanding—really shaped how I think.

Competitions added a different element. They encouraged focus and persistence, but they also made it tempting to judge yourself by whether you could solve a problem faster than someone else. So there were two sides to it: the joy of discovering a solution, and the pressure to prove that you were good.

Looking back, I think the most valuable part was becoming comfortable with being stuck. Not knowing the answer doesn’t necessarily mean you can’t get there. Sometimes you just need another approach. What I’ve had to learn since then is that, outside programming competitions, deciding which problem matters can be harder than solving it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think learning to program early gave me a habit of breaking a big problem into smaller pieces. When something doesn’t work, you have to ask where your understanding went wrong, change one thing, and try again. That became a way of thinking beyond programming, too.

Competitions added a different element: working under pressure and realizing that being stuck doesn’t mean you can’t solve something. Sometimes you just need another approach. But they can also make you impatient for a clear answer. In a competition, the problem is defined for you. Later, you discover that deciding which problem is worth solving can be the harder part.

So I’d say the biggest influence was a combination of persistence and independence—the feeling that I could explore something on my own and gradually figure it out.
